note: Although preserves contrast; since and so invent opposite causal relations. Feedback distinguishes both. Replace “keeps that relationship” with a direct question about strength and drawback.
Addition is explicitly required; contrast and consequence are legitimate connectors elsewhere. Feedback correctly explains each choice. Good Bronze recognition.
B meets both reason-first and punctuation requirements. A omits the boundary comma; C is correctly written but result-first. Feedback does not mislabel C ungrammatical.
C alone closes the first sentence and offsets initial “However”. The feedback confines the comma advice to this use. Useful Bronze punctuation comparison.
B separates the past visit from current availability; A limits the offer to the past and C introduces repeated visits. Feedback makes all three time readings explicit.
Only A supplies two complete sentences, but “long” shifts from waiting time to possible queue length. Use wording about taking a while consistently; retain splice and fragment distractors.
Naming the space display removes the ambiguity of “there”; “both” changes the fact. Feedback diagnoses the two distinct errors. Clear Bronze reference.
B is the only present-tense answer with agreement. C also agrees with its subject, because past “gave” works with singular subjects. Ask specifically about agreement in the present tense.

The key changes “cannot use the discount” into “cannot go”, potentially to the cinema at all. Offer an option explicitly retaining usual inability to use the offer. Keep a defensible timing change in the distractors.
A identifies a subset; B and C treat coaching as shared by all courses. The explanation is sound. Ask which wording makes clear that only coached courses cost extra.
C links stopping outside to saving the walk and leaves arrival timing independent. A reverses causation and B adds a second effect. Strong Silver application with useful feedback.
B preserves the evaluation and follows “despite” with a noun phrase. A changes emphasis and C uses a finite clause. Replace “retains that evaluation” with “still says the writer liked the sound”.
C preserves the stated limitation. A is less precise and B explicitly applies the claim to both. Feedback highlights that clarity alone does not preserve meaning.
So signals an enabling cause; then gives sequence and also adds information. Feedback makes possible uses explicit. Suitable comparison for Silver.

B fixes the comma splice without changing time or cause. A invents a cause and C changes the time. Replace “repairs the boundary” with “corrects the punctuation”; keep comparison with alternate valid edits in feedback.
C joins the lift observations and signals the new location. A invents a consequence and B offers a misleading reference. Good multi-step Silver comparison.

B preserves cause and the limited view problem. A widens the criticism and C misconnects the ideas. Ask directly how the blanket helped and which seats had the problem. Master should require explaining the edit or making one independently.
Check both sides of the contrast, then compare one-sentence “although” and two-sentence “however”. The feedback models both accurately. Three-word entry can omit the contrast entirely.

The instructions are the reason and independent completion is the result. Match the pair then mark the introductory clause boundary. The explanation already teaches both; a short generic entry proves neither.
Match current discount versus past availability; do not require a three-word response. Keep the clear visit/offer time contrast, and move the book/film tense note to a relevant example.
Let learners select what “these activities” refers to and compare repetition with a clear reference. The note explains “that” and the anaphor, but the three-word gate can bypass both.

Check “they” and “each” against the levels first, then invite a short comparison of the sentences. Preserve the distinct emphasis explained in feedback. An answer naming just “the short levels” should not have to be padded.

Replacing the verb alone leaves an ungrammatical Saturday sentence. Compare “last Saturday I visited” with “I visit on Saturdays” and check the one-off/habit distinction. Feedback supplies this contrast already.
Select sandwiches and cake, then optionally substitute the nouns. The key explains why “both” avoids repetition. Learners should not have to reach seven words to name two items.

Useful controlled writing; the model retains crowding and friendly staff. Compare the split and original sentences after an attempt. Mark this self-review, with a check that “However” starts the second sentence.
The advice still makes sense without “However”. Ask learners to compare the explicit qualification with simple addition. Use a checked choice rather than a generic length gate.
The match is useful: visit then, distance now. Feedback calls the distance “directions”, which is inaccurate. Let learners label each fact by time and compare another present-tense detail.
The open rewrite is worthwhile as self-review. The two sentences preserve texture and contrast in emphasis. Clarify which sentence to split and include the original and rewrite together.
The sample shows the rewritten second half but omits the earlier queue clause. Display both phases together and ask learners to preserve both. Use rewrite/self-review rather than a checked mark.
The model removes the condition, making the advice appear broader. Use a two-version audience comparison and an optional rewrite. Seven words are unrelated to identifying the affected readers.
Yet preserves the unexpected enjoyment; so invents a cause. Ask which connector suits the ideas and show them side by side. Feedback explains both, and a length gate adds little.
Retain productive rewriting, with the full two-sentence revision in the model. Naming the explorers avoids ambiguity and relative “whose” ties evidence closer to the judgement. Mark self-review.

The sample gives the positive soundtrack the main emphasis. Ask students to underline the main judgement in the revised sentence rather than identify a term unsupported by examples. Check comparison and self-review the rewrite.

Move “however” and check the one initial comma against the original parenthetical pair. A small punctuation interaction is more focused than seven words; use as optional reinforcement if already secure.
Who refers to the photographer. Display the complete alternative with “she”, including the investigation clause. Select the referent, then discuss how splitting delays the plot detail.
Two sentences with “as a result” preserve vivid description and imagined presence. Name the exact source sentence to split and provide a self-review check for the cause/effect relationship.

The similar-character problem is in the preceding paragraph. Show it alongside the verdict, then check the reference and the despite contrast. Completing the visible extract alone cannot identify the cause.

The speaker wants to discover bands; the classmates’ motives are unstated. The model is clear but “finite verb” distracts from the intended point. Ask learners to check the subject and self-review their rewrite.
Between concerts adds timing that also lacks. A checked distinction between timing and addition is enough. Make optional alongside similar connector recognition.
The example preserves the queue-to-discomfort effect, but “this” needs a clear antecedent. Ask the learner to compare “this” with “the wait”, then self-review a two-sentence version.
The clause gives the reason for arriving early without guaranteeing a spot. Check purpose versus result, with an example of each. A seven-word response can pass without making that distinction.
The commas enclose optional details about opening and location. “What could be removed” allows other deletions. Ask learners to select the part between commas and compare the resulting main claim.

This refers to the demonstration, not one activity or the instructors themselves. The sample shows the whole-clause reference well. Combine this with Summer Sound’s “this” comparison or make one optional.

The model preserves all equipment and repeated attempts at most courses. Label the grammar contrast as examples rather than exhaustive rules. Keep an independent short rewrite and self-check the restriction “most”.
“Rather than” signals a substitute. Simply inserting and before “relying” creates a mismatch, not a coherent new recommendation. Compare complete parallel sentences rather than a word swap.

Players are intended to collect tools, but the avatar makes the ambiguity authentic. Ask learners to make the intended agent clear using two complete versions. Name the actor explicitly in model and feedback.
The instructions require “This”, but the example uses “That gradual progression”. Allow either or model the requested construction. Retain experience in reordering claim and reason, with self-review.
“Helps” can express a general claim and need not establish that a clearer tutorial already exists. Compare “would help” with “the new tutorial now helps” to isolate the intended inference.
The instructions problem is outside the displayed ending. Show the source alongside the recommendation. Check what “that frustration” refers to before explaining the despite contrast.
The completed visit and continuing view are a useful mixed-tense pair. The model gives only the rewritten opening. Display the complete sentence and compare with Willow Kitchen or make one optional.
Good contrast rewrite with the praise and exact limitation intact. It duplicates Riverside’s although/however transformation. Use one for instruction and the other for independent self-review.

The clause qualifies the weekday choice via fewer visitors and more access. Match the time and the reason. Feedback says “fewer people means”; use standard plural agreement or “having fewer people means”.
The sample fits 45–65, preserves both contrasts, the twenty-minute wait and late lesson, and shows each checklist target. Retain as a broad Gold revision, with checklist as self-review.

The model is 36 words against about 40–60 and repeats enjoyment after asking learners to reduce repetition. Keep yesterday’s experience distinct from ongoing game features. Model economical cohesion and align the target with the example.

Accurate ¥70/¥50 comparison and a qualified reader effect within 35–55 words. The present-tense linked statements support a useful transfer from correction to original review writing. Checklist matches the response.
Model fits the range and uses past workshop events and a present assessment. The reason and pronouns remain clear; the three checks connect directly to the brief. Preserve self-review.

The model meets the range and keeps sequence and bus deadline. “Leave promptly” implies reaching the stop is feasible, but no walking time is supplied. Keep it as timing information and advise checking the walk before booking.

The independent edit preserves the route, timed lights and limited view of signs, and exemplifies appropriate tense. Specify that 60–80 words apply to the extract only. The example also corrects “although … but” although not named in the editor’s note; clarify that students should identify priorities and still fix other issues.
